week.t: NASA: second spacewalk Thu 5 Nov, 8:30 am EST (9:30 pm SGT), fits the eighth and last roll-out solar array
ISRO: Aditya-L1’s VELC shows a 5 Aug 2024 solar eruption expanded lopsidedly, mapped in 3D from one spacecraft
NASA Earth Observatory: 25 named storms in the NW Pacific since April; Champi peaked near 300 km/h
Science News Explores: a python’s heart can balloon up to 25% in a day; the Grinch’s would have collapsed
NASA: Swift expected to re-enter on Wednesday 4 Nov, 22 years after launch; risk to anyone 1 in 2,100

tiles.cap: 9:30 pm tomorrow: two astronauts unroll the last of eight new solar wings on the ISS
tiles.nums: The station’s power-generating capacity before and after the roll-out arrays, a job begun in June 2021
tiles.p1: The second and final spacewalk of this pair is scheduled to start at 8:30 am US Eastern time on Thursday 5 November, which is 9:30 pm in Singapore. Flight engineers Joshua Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency and Anil Menon of NASA will install the eighth and final roll-out solar array on the station’s starboard truss. Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney will help them into their suits, monitor the pair and operate the Canadarm2 robotic arm from inside.
tiles.p2: Why now: the first walk of the pair, on 29 October, ran 7 hours 11 minutes; this one finishes a power upgrade that began in June 2021.
deep: The job

The new arrays unroll over the station’s original solar wings. Since June 2021 crews have been adding them to raise the station’s power-generating capacity from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts. The 29 October walk fitted the seventh array; Thursday’s is the eighth and last.
Who is outside
For Kutryk, the 29 October walk was his first; for Menon it was his fourth. NASA counted it as US spacewalk 100 and the 285th spacewalk in support of station assembly, maintenance and upgrades.
Watching it

NASA says live continuous coverage begins at 7 am on Thursday, US Eastern time, which is 8 pm in Singapore, with the walk itself due to start 90 minutes later. The first walk in the pair lasted 7 hours 11 minutes.
Meanwhile inside

A Dragon cargo ship is expected to return to Earth in mid-November packed with completed science experiments. In the Russian segment, station commander Pyotr Dubrov was installing Earth-observation gear and flight engineer Anna Kikina was transferring water from the Progress 96 cargo craft.
tiles.src: NASA Space Station blog, 3 Nov 2026 (Mark A. Garcia) · NASA Space Station blog, 29 Oct 2026 (Mark A. Garcia)

tiles.cap: India’s Aditya-L1 caught a solar eruption that did not grow like a bubble. It was lopsided
tiles.nums: Solar radii from the Sun’s centre: the ring of corona shown by VELC, Aditya-L1’s coronagraph, in ISRO’s image of the eruption
tiles.p1: ISRO reported on 3 November that a coronal mass ejection observed on 5 August 2024 did not expand outward from the Sun like a simple symmetric bubble, as previously thought. Instead it underwent non-uniform expansion and developed an asymmetric shape. The result comes from VELC, the Visible Emission Line Coronagraph on Aditya-L1, India’s Sun-watching spacecraft, in work by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics in Bengaluru.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: a CME aimed at Earth can disrupt satellites and communications, and whether it expands evenly changes how the solar wind drags on it, so when it arrives.
deep: What a CME is
A coronal mass ejection is a massive burst of hot, magnetised plasma released from the Sun’s outer atmosphere. Most coronagraphs can only image it in two dimensions, as motion across the sky.
The speed-gun trick

VELC uses Doppler spectroscopy, which ISRO says works on the same principle as traffic speed guns. During the 5 August 2024 CME it detected two Doppler-shifted branches on opposite sides of the normal coronal emission line: plasma coming toward the observer and plasma moving away, in the same eruption.
Why lopsided

A symmetrically expanding CME shell could not reproduce the observed spectral pattern. Once the team’s three-dimensional model added asymmetric sideways expansion and a tilt, the simulated spectra matched the VELC observations.
One spacecraft, three dimensions

Working out a CME’s 3D shape normally needs several spacecraft looking from different angles. The authors say this shows VELC can constrain the three-dimensional geometry of an eruption from a single vantage point. The paper, by Saurabh Tripathi, Tanmoy Samanta and Jayant Joshi, is in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
tiles.src: ISRO, 3 Nov 2026 · Indian Institute of Astrophysics, Bengaluru · The Astrophysical Journal Letters
tiles.credit: Image: ISRO / IIA, Aditya-L1 VELC, with NASA SDO/AIA

tiles.cap: 25 named storms on, the Pacific is still churning: a super typhoon and a parade of storms
tiles.nums: Typhoon Champi’s maximum sustained winds, nearly 185 mph, before its remnants reached Alaska
tiles.p1: NASA’s Earth Observatory says tropical cyclone activity in the Northwest Pacific has been elevated since April 2026, when Sinlaku surged to super typhoon strength and battered Micronesia, Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands. Twenty-five named storms later, the basin still hummed with activity in late October. On 29 October the EPIC camera on the DSCOVR satellite caught Super Typhoon In-fa near the Mariana Islands while the remnants of Typhoon Champi approached Alaska amid a parade of storms moving across the Bering Sea.
tiles.p2: Why: a strong El Niño is under way in the Pacific, a likely contributor, and El Niño shifts storms toward Guam, the Northern Marianas, Japan and the Korean Peninsula.
deep: A rare shape

In-fa showed traits of an annular storm: these typically lack the prominent outer spiral rainbands. Annular storms are rare, just 4 percent of tropical cyclones in the western North Pacific, and their eyes average about 45 kilometres across.
Champi

Champi reached maximum sustained winds of nearly 300 kilometres per hour. It narrowly skirted Taiwan and Guam but still brought damaging winds and intense rain to both, and to parts of China and Japan.
Typhoons in Alaska

Champi is the fourth ex-typhoon to enter Alaskan waters this year, after Bang-Lang in August, Dujuan in September and Choi-wan in early October. Roughly 60 ex-typhoons have affected the state since 1970; the autumns of 1997 and 2015, both very strong El Niño years, had three each.
Fifth for the Marianas
In-fa is the fifth typhoon to affect the Mariana Islands this year. El Niño emerges roughly every two to seven years and changes where Pacific storms form and travel.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, 3 Nov 2026 (story by Adam Voiland, images by Michala Garrison)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison, DSCOVR EPIC

tiles.cap: Make a sunset in a jar: shine a torch through milky water and the far end turns orange
tiles.nums: Blue light is scattered roughly ten times more than red by the molecules of the air
tiles.p1: Fill a clear container with water, shine a torch through it from one end, and add milk a few drops at a time until the beam shows. From the side the beam looks bluish-white; from the end it looks yellow-orange. You have made the sky and a sunset in one jar: the milk makes the beam visible, and the light scatters the way sunlight does off air molecules, with short blue wavelengths scattered far more than long red ones.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: the scattered blue is what you see when you look up; the red that was not scattered keeps going straight, and that is a sunset.
deep: Why blue

Sunlight is white light holding every colour, each with its own wavelength. As it crosses the atmosphere it collides with gas molecules and is scattered, and shorter wavelengths scatter more: the Exploratorium puts blue at approximately ten times red. Violet scatters even more, but the Sun emits much less violet, so the sky looks blue.
Why orange

At sunset the light travels a longer path through the atmosphere, so most of the blue is scattered out before it reaches you and what is left looks reddish orange. In the jar, the far end of the beam is the sunset: add enough milk and you can watch the beam shift from blue-white to yellow-orange along its length.
The test
Hold a white card at the far end of the container to catch the orange spot on it. If you have added enough milk, you can see the beam itself shift from blue-white to yellow-orange along its length.
Going further

Scattering polarises light, because light is a transverse wave. Put a lens from polarised sunglasses between torch and jar and rotate it: a friend watching from the top sees the beam brighten as you, watching from the side, see it dim, and the other way round.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Blue Sky (Exploratorium Teacher Institute)

tiles.cap: The Moon is falling. Every second it drops about 1/20 of an inch, and keeps missing Earth
tiles.nums: How much weaker gravity is at the Moon, 60 times farther from Earth’s centre than we are: 1 over 60 squared
tiles.p1: Feynman’s arithmetic: an object dropped near the Earth’s surface falls 16 feet in its first second. The Moon is 240,000 miles away, 60 times as far from the Earth’s centre as we are, and Newton’s law says gravity weakens with the square of the distance, so the Moon should fall only 1/3600 of 16 feet each second, which is roughly 1/20 of an inch. Measure how far the Moon’s orbit curves away from a straight line in one second and you get the same 1/20 of an inch.
tiles.p2: Why it feels wrong: the Moon never gets any closer. It falls, Feynman says, in the sense that it falls away from the straight line it would follow if there were no forces.
deep: The 27-day clock
The Moon goes around the Earth in approximately 27 days. From the size of its orbit and that period you can work out how far it deviates from a straight line in one second: roughly 1/20 of an inch.
Newton’s near miss

Newton first found a discrepancy so large that he regarded the theory as contradicted by the facts. Later a new measurement of the size of the Earth showed that astronomers had been using an incorrect distance to the Moon; with the right number the calculation gave beautiful agreement.
A number that is deep

Compare gravity with electricity: the gravitational attraction between two electrons, relative to their electrical repulsion, is 1 divided by 4.17 × 10⁴². Feynman: this fantastic number is a natural constant, so it involves something deep in nature.
What gravity is

Feynman is blunt: no one has since given any machinery behind the law of gravity. The law says what gravity does, and why mathematics can describe nature without a mechanism behind it, he says, no one knows.
tiles.src: The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 7: The Theory of Gravitation (Caltech)

tiles.cap: Garmin’s Cirqa is a fitness tracker with no screen at all: a 14.8 g puck on a fabric strap
tiles.nums: Garmin’s battery claim; TechRadar’s reviewer got a solid week with three or four workouts
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes the Cirqa, a screenless band from Garmin. The engineering is in subtraction: no display, a 27 × 47 × 9 mm module weighing 14.8 g in a fibre-reinforced polymer case, a fabric strap, Bluetooth and ANT+ radios, an accelerometer, a wrist-based heart-rate sensor and a Pulse Ox blood-oxygen sensor, 128 MB of memory and a 5 ATM water rating, which Garmin defines as withstanding pressure equal to a depth of 50 m. Garmin’s suggested price is US$199.99.
tiles.p2: Why TIME picked it: rival screenless wearables, it says, normalised paywalled health insights, and Garmin’s Jill Kaiser says it gives you your insights without locking you into additional prices.
deep: What is inside

The radio spec is in the manual: 2400–2483.5 MHz at under 13 dBm, the 2.4 GHz band. It works from −20 °C to 60 °C but charges only between 0 °C and 45 °C. The battery is a built-in rechargeable lithium-ion cell; Garmin does not publish its capacity.
No GPS

There is no GPS inside; routes come from your phone. A dedicated side button starts and stops your most common activity without the phone, and it auto-detects activities longer than 15 minutes. TechRadar found the heart-rate sensor within 1–3 beats per minute of a Polar H10 chest strap, with one outlier of about 10 bpm.
What reviewers found wrong

TechRadar’s Matt Evans (6 August 2026) listed limited metrics compared with a full Garmin watch, a relatively high price for the puck, a bicep band sold separately, and coaching features locked behind a paywall on top of the upfront cost: Garmin Connect+ at US$6.99 a month. Tom’s Guide found the strap the scratchiest of the bunch and noted it costs twice the Fitbit Air, US$199 against US$99.
The battery race

Tom’s Guide puts the Whoop 5.0 at roughly two weeks between charges against about ten days for the Cirqa, and the Fitbit Air at 5.2 g against the Cirqa’s 14.8 g. Lighter and longer-lasting are the two numbers every screenless band is chasing.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Hannah Singleton) · Garmin spec page and owner’s manual · TechRadar review, 6 Aug 2026 (Matt Evans) · Tom’s Guide, 8 Aug 2026 (Dan Bracaglia)

tiles.cap: An NUS rig caught 400 kg of CO₂ a day from a waste plant’s exhaust. Next: 5 tonnes a day
tiles.nums: Awarded to five scale-up projects, three of them from NUS, announced on 23 October
tiles.p1: Three NUS teams from the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering have won Low Carbon Energy Research scale-up grants, among five projects sharing S$65 million from Singapore’s Advanced Energy and Decarbonisation Office. Professor Zhao Dan’s capture system, tested at a waste-to-energy research facility, captured around 400 kilogrammes of carbon dioxide a day with close to 100 per cent recovery; the next phase is designed for five tonnes a day from higher-concentration flue gas.
tiles.p2: Why here: the awards were announced at the first Singapore Industry Decarbonisation Forum on 23 October, with Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong as guest of honour.
deep: Capture at the power plant
A separate pilot by Zhao’s team at YTL PowerSeraya’s natural-gas combined-cycle plant targets two tonnes of carbon dioxide a day, and the group is working with Chevron to evaluate capture materials.
Hydrogen without the CO₂

Associate Professor Sibudjing Kawi’s team, with Siemens and PacificLight Power, splits methane in a catalytic membrane reactor at a relatively low 500 to 600 degrees Celsius. The first phase produced 500 litres of hydrogen a day and a prototype designed for one kilogramme of hydrogen and three kilogrammes of carbon nanotubes daily; the next aims at 100 kilogrammes of hydrogen and 300 kilogrammes of nanotubes a day.
Membranes

Associate Professor Zhang Sui’s hollow-fibre membranes captured around four kilogrammes of carbon dioxide a day in small modules; the scale-up is a modular pilot able to process up to 1 ton of flue gas per day.
What the grant is
The scale-up grant gives follow-on support to projects that achieved promising outcomes under an earlier LCER programme. All three NUS leads are in the College of Design and Engineering.

tiles.cap: An A*STAR AI cuts errors in long DNA reads 100-fold: 32 of 46 chromosomes read end to end
tiles.nums: Human chromosomes reconstructed telomere to telomere, repetitive stretches included, after HERRO cleaned the reads
tiles.p1: Ultra-long nanopore reads of DNA are powerful but error-prone. HERRO, a deep-learning algorithm from A*STAR’s Genome Institute of Singapore with the University of Zagreb and Oxford Nanopore Technologies, learns to correct those errors and reduced them by up to 100-fold in human genomes. With the cleaned reads the team reconstructed up to 32 of the 46 chromosomes end to end, including highly repetitive sections.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: the repetitive parts of the genome are the hardest to assemble, and they are where long reads earn their keep.
deep: The method

HERRO is a deep-learning model trained to spot and fix the characteristic mistakes in ultra-long nanopore sequences, while keeping the reads at their full length so they still carry long-range information.
Who
The first author is Dominik Stanojević; the senior researcher is Mile Šikić of A*STAR’s Genome Institute of Singapore, who did his PhD at the University of Zagreb in 2008.
Where
The work is published in Nature, volume 655, pages 158–165 (2026).

tiles.cap: Would a heart that grew three sizes make you strong? A python’s can swell 25% in a day
tiles.nums: How much a python’s heart can balloon in a day after it eats, then shrink back once the meal is digested
tiles.p1: Science News Explores asked heart scientists about the Grinch, whose heart grows three sizes and who then, in the 1966 film, gains the strength of ten Grinches plus two. Heart size is generally pegged to body size, says cardiologist Michelle Kittleson: bigger people tend to have bigger hearts. Some animals really do grow theirs fast: when pythons eat, their hearts can balloon by up to 25 percent in a day, and larger hearts pump blood with more force. But a human heart that suddenly inflated would be too big to pump blood; Kittleson says the Grinch would have keeled over and collapsed.
tiles.p2: Why it is more than a joke: a 2025 analysis of records from more than 360,000 people in Australia found those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years.
deep: Python hearts

Leslie Leinwand, a molecular biologist and geneticist at the University of Colorado Boulder, works on pythons. The bigger the meal, the more the heart grows, and it shrinks back once the meal is digested; her team reported the finding in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences in 2024. Whether it makes the snakes stronger overall, they do not know.
The good kind of big

With hard, regular training, Leinwand says, your heart gets bigger, but in a good way. Kittleson: an athlete’s heart gets bigger and thicker, and that helps them pump more blood per minute than someone with a normal-size heart.
The bad kind

The one rare condition in which a heart inflates suddenly is takotsubo, or stress cardiomyopathy. A surge of epinephrine, also called adrenaline, from extreme stress can make the heart chamber bulge, and that causes immediate heart failure as the heart gets too big to pump blood.
The data

The Australian analysis, in JACC: Advances, looked at medical records from more than 360,000 people. Those with smaller-than-average hearts had a higher risk of dying within five years than people with average or larger hearts.
tiles.src: Science News Explores, 3 Nov 2026 (Tina Hesman Saey) · JACC: Advances, 2025 · PNAS, 2024

tiles.cap: September’s oceans ran 1.10 °C above average, the biggest departure of any month on record
tiles.nums: Global ocean surface in September 2026 above the 20th-century average: the highest for any month NOAA has recorded
tiles.p1: NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information report that September 2026 was the second-warmest September in a record that starts in 1850, 1.33 °C above the 20th-century average and 0.07 °C behind 2023. The ocean surface was 1.10 °C above average, the highest departure for any month on record, with persistent El Niño conditions driving record warmth across the central and eastern tropical Pacific.
tiles.p2: Connects to: the same El Niño that NASA’s experts call a likely contributor to the Pacific’s crowded typhoon year.
deep: Land and ice

Land surfaces were 1.83 °C above average, the third-highest September in the 177-year record. Global sea-ice extent was 8.54 million square miles, 800,000 square miles below the 1991–2020 average and the third-smallest September in the 48-year record.
Storms

The globe produced 19 tropical storms in September; nine reached cyclone strength and six became major cyclones. The Atlantic managed four tropical storms and no hurricanes, the first time in the satellite era that no hurricane formed before October.
The year so far
January to September 2026 ranks second-highest on record behind 2024, and NOAA says 2026 is very likely to land among the five warmest years, with second-warmest the most probable outcome.
tiles.src: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information, Monitoring Global Temperature and Precipitation in September 2026 (9 Oct 2026)

tiles.cap: MIT’s phrase for what a chatbot answer gives you: “the illusion of learning”
tiles.nums: principles in MIT’s 2026 report on AI in education
tiles.p1: MIT’s report does not ban AI. One of its eight principles is augmentation, not automation: AI should be used to “augment and enhance curiosity, creativity, and learning, not automate them.” Its named risks are the ones you would expect, weaker memory and confidence, falling back on AI at the first hint of struggle, and one you might not: fewer people. MIT saw fewer students at office hours and, anecdotally, fewer in-person groups in dorms and libraries, turning to AI instead of to classmates, TAs or professors.
tiles.p2: The point: the product of school is you, not the mark.
deep: What MIT asks of its own students
Learn to write good prompts, check every output, recognise when it has made something up, and know when not to use it at all.
Why checking matters
The report warns that models hallucinate, so students need to learn when an output is likely to be made up. MIT’s rule for research: a human verifies, and AI is never listed as a co-author.
Keep it human

The report says every subject should include a regular in-person social component, calls for more project-based work, and asks for deliberately AI-free experiences and AI-free spaces for interaction and assessment.
tiles.src: MIT Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training, Aug 2026

tiles.cap: Swift, built for 2 years, watched the sky for 22. On Wednesday it falls out of it
tiles.nums: NASA’s estimate of the risk that a surviving piece harms anyone on Earth
tiles.p1: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory is expected to re-enter Earth’s atmosphere on Wednesday 4 November, almost 22 years after launch. As of Monday the US Space Force predicted that the roughly 3,200-pound (about 1,450 kg) spacecraft will come down at about 3:30 am US Eastern time, which is 4:30 pm in Singapore, with an uncertainty of 11 hours. NASA expects most of it to burn up, but some components are expected to survive.
tiles.p2: Why here: because Swift orbits at a low tilt, any surviving fragments can only land between 20.6° south and 20.6° north. Singapore, at about 1.3° north, sits inside that band.
deep: What Swift did

Swift launched in 2004 to catch gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the cosmos, and was designed for a two-year prime mission. It kept working for more than two decades of science operations.
The odds
NASA puts the risk of harm to anyone on Earth at approximately 1 in 2,100. That is the chance for the whole planet combined; for any one person it is a tiny fraction of that.
The band

Swift’s orbit has a low inclination, so NASA says re-entry locations of surviving fragments are limited to between 20.6 degrees south and 20.6 degrees north latitude. Everywhere outside that band is out of the question.
Watch the update
NASA and the Space Force say they will keep monitoring the re-entry and updating the prediction, so the Wednesday-afternoon estimate for Singapore could move by hours either way.
tiles.src: NASA Swift blog, 2 Nov 2026 (Alise Fisher, Goddard)

tiles.cap: Two fridge-sized probes skim Earth on Saturday evening, fire engines, and leave for Mars
tiles.nums: the length of each trans-Mars injection burn, adding more than 1,000 mph (about 1,600 km/h)
tiles.p1: NASA’s twin ESCAPADE spacecraft will each perform a manoeuvre no agency spacecraft has flown before, a powered flyby of Earth, one after the other. The first makes its closest approach and finishes its engine burn around 5 am US Eastern on Saturday 7 November, which is 6 pm in Singapore; the second follows around 6 am Eastern on Monday 9 November, 7 pm here. Each burn is made over southern Australia and raises the craft’s speed from about 6.3 to about 6.7 miles per second (roughly 10.1 to 10.8 km/s).
tiles.p2: Why now: ESCAPADE launched in November 2025 when Earth and Mars were on opposite sides of the Sun, so the pair looped around Earth–Sun Lagrange point 2 in a loiter orbit, waiting for the right moment to be thrown onward.
deep: How close

Closest approach is between 600 and 1,100 miles (roughly 970 to 1,770 km) above the surface. At the speed they leave, NASA says, the spacecraft could fly from Washington, DC, to San Francisco in less than 7 minutes, about Mach 30 to Mach 31.
Then the long cruise

After the flybys comes a 10-month cruise. Arrival at Mars is set for 7 and 9 September 2027, where the pair will be the first multi-spacecraft mission to fly in formation around the planet, measuring how the solar wind strips away the Martian atmosphere.
Bonus science on the way
While loitering, the spacecraft flew through a distant part of Earth’s magnetotail, the long magnetic wake the solar wind drags out behind our planet. NASA says those findings will be shared soon.
Can you see them
NASA says the spacecraft are faint and a telescope will most likely be needed; the coordinates come from JPL’s Horizons system. Each one is about the size of a standard refrigerator.
tiles.src: NASA ESCAPADE blog, 2 Nov 2026 (Vanessa Thomas, Goddard)
tiles.credit: Image: Advanced Space / Matt Bolliger, via NASA

tiles.cap: Mars and Jupiter pass 1.2° apart on 15–16 November, and three supermoons start on the 24th
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors at best, before dawn on 17–18 November, after the Moon has set
tiles.p1: NASA’s What’s Up for November 2026, presented by Raquel Villanueva of JPL: the Southern Taurids peak around 5 November with occasional bright fireballs; the Northern Taurids around the 12th at about five meteors an hour; Mars and Jupiter appear about 1.2 degrees apart before sunrise on 15–16 November, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish; and the Leonids run before dawn on 17–18 November, up to around 15 an hour under ideal skies.
tiles.p2: Why here: Singapore sits almost on the equator, so Mars and Jupiter rise steeply in the east before dawn, and a full Moon on 24 November, the first of three supermoons in a row, climbs high overhead.
deep: Moon phases

Third quarter 1 November, new Moon on the 8th, first quarter on the 17th, full supermoon on the 24th, third quarter again on the 30th. The new Moon week, 5–12 November, is the dark window for the Taurids.
1.2 degrees

A common rule of thumb: your little finger at arm’s length covers about one degree of sky. Mars and Jupiter will sit about a finger apart, close enough to share a view in binoculars but easy to tell apart by colour.
A light-day away
On 17 November NASA marks Voyager 1 becoming the first human-made object one light-day from Earth: a radio message sent that day takes a full 24 hours to reach it.
Seeing meteors

NASA’s advice for the Leonids: find a dark location and give your eyes about half an hour to adjust. In Singapore that means a dark park or beach with an open eastern sky in the hours before dawn, once the Moon has set.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A phone screen only its owner can read: two kinds of pixels, and the wide ones switch off
tiles.nums: peak brightness measured by Tom’s Guide, against 1,860 on last year’s S25 Ultra: dimmer, even with privacy off
tiles.p1: The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra made TIME’s Best Inventions of 2026 list as “a privacy-focused smartphone”. Its 6.9-inch display has two different kinds of pixels, narrow and wide; in privacy mode the wide pixels turn off, which limits what can be seen from the side, with no stick-on filter. Samsung lists it at 214 g, 7.9 mm thick, with a 5,000 mAh battery, a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip, a 200-megapixel main camera and an Armor Aluminum frame.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: Tom’s Guide measured 1,806 nits peak against 1,860 for last year’s S25 Ultra, dimmer across the board even with privacy off, and listed narrower viewing angles, a camera bump that makes the phone wobble when laid flat, and still no Qi2 magnets.
deep: The engineering

Samsung describes the feature as controlling the screen’s viewing angle to limit peripheral vision, and calls it the world’s first Privacy Display on mobile. TechRadar’s description: the panel has narrow and wide pixels, and in privacy mode the wide pixels turn off. It can be set for the whole screen or only for PINs, passwords and notification pop-ups, and per app.
What the lab found

Tom’s Guide measured 586 nits with Maximum Privacy on and 588 with it off, so the person holding the phone loses almost nothing. The whole panel, though, is dimmer than before: 1,209 nits in auto-brightness against 1,231 on the S25 Ultra, while Samsung rates it at up to 2,600 nits.
Complaints

By mid-March some owners were reporting blurry lettering, eye strain and headaches on Reddit; Tom’s Guide noted it was not clear how widespread the problem was, or whether it was the privacy feature or the panel itself. Samsung’s suggested fixes were dark mode, extra dim and Eye Comfort Shield.
The rest of the phone

TechRadar’s review calls it Samsung’s best Galaxy S phone yet but an iterative update, with no more titanium frame and no MagSafe-style magnets. Battery life in Tom’s Guide’s web test: 16 h 10 min, nearly two hours more than the S25 Ultra. Price $1,299.99.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 · Samsung spec page · Tom’s Guide review and lab tests, March 2026 · TechRadar review, 2 Mar 2026

tiles.cap: Stare at the black dot: the blue blur beside it quietly vanishes. Move your eyes: back
tiles.nums: the size of the paper dot in the Exploratorium’s version, seen through waxed paper until its edges blur
tiles.p1: Look at the small black dot on this tile and keep your eyes and head perfectly still. The fuzzy blue patch next to it fades until it blends into the pink, and it comes back the moment you move your eyes. The Exploratorium’s Fading Dot snack does it with a 1-inch (2.5 cm) blue paper dot on pink paper under a sheet of waxed paper, lifted until the blue is very faint.
tiles.p2: What is going on: your eyes make tiny jittering movements all the time, and each movement sends new information to the brain. A blurred edge changes so gradually that the jitter brings nothing new, so the brain stops reporting it. If the dot had a distinct border your eyes would immediately detect the change.
deep: Why the rest stays sharp
Everything else on the page keeps its crisp edges, so every micro-movement refreshes it. Only the thing with no edge can slip away.
Fog

The Exploratorium notes a 2003 paper in the Proceedings of the International Joint Conference on Neural Networks reporting that moving cars seem to slow down in foggy conditions: low contrast reduces perceived speed.
Make your own

Cut a 2.5 cm blue dot, put it in the centre of a pink sheet, lay waxed paper on top and lift the waxed paper toward your face until the blue is just a faint smudge. Then fix your gaze beside it. Try other colour pairs.
Related

This is a cousin of the afterimage: both come from your visual system adapting to anything that does not change. The difference is that here nothing is burned in; the signal simply stops being reported.
